Alarm over Southern Rhodesia runs through Resolution 1883, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 14 October 1963. The Assembly had studied the British colony, where a white minority regime held power under a constitution most of the people had no fair part in choosing. It recalls the 1960 call to end colonial rule and two past votes on the same land.

The text calls racial bias a breach of the Charter's core pledges, fit to be condemned wherever it occurs. It notes that the UN's decolonization team had flagged the worsening, explosive state of the territory to the Security Council. The record shows the Assembly pressing Britain, the ruling power, to hand power to the majority.
un-ga-res-a-69-83: Joint work with the Council of Europe fills Resolution A/69/83, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The two bodies first struck a deal in 1951, and the Council has sat as an observer at the Assembly since 1989. The text praises the Council's work for human rights, free rule, and the rule of law across Europe, through its norms, checks, and watch bodies. Its part in the growth of world law is noted as well.
un-sc-res-183:
Resolution 183 returns to the question of the territories under Portuguese rule, after the Secretary-General tried to open talks between Portugal and African states. The text was adopted on 11 December 1963, though the catalog record gives 1964. The contact failed to produce agreement on what self-determination means.

The Council regrets that failure and deprecates Portugal's refusal to comply with Resolution 180. It restates the meaning of self-determination from Assembly Resolution 1514: all peoples have the right to choose their political status freely and to pursue their own economic, social, and cultural growth. It also notes the territories' listing as Non-Self-Governing Territories.
un-sc-res-1383: This library holds Resolution 1383 as an official Council record, dated 2001 in its catalog. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1483:
Resolution 1483 is the Security Council's main Iraq decision from the weeks after Saddam Hussein's government fell in 2003. Adopted that May, it lifted the trade sanctions placed on Iraq during the 1990s. It also set the legal frame for the country under occupation.

Inside, the Council recognizes the United States and Britain as occupying powers with duties toward Iraqi civilians. It ends the old oil-for-food limits, calls for Iraqi oil money to fund rebuilding, and backs a UN role in forming a new government. Readers get the exact terms on which postwar Iraq was first organized.
un-sc-res-1783: Security Council Resolution 1783 survives in official-record form in this collection, transcribed by English Wikisource. Resolutions are filed by number and cited by number, and 1783 is this act's permanent place. Within it, the members state their grounds and then their decision, in the sequence the Charter's practice has made standard.
un-sc-res-1883:
For another year, Resolution 1883 renewed the UN mission in Iraq in 2009. UNAMI's advisers were helping Iraqis run elections, settle disputes over internal borders, and bring refugees home. The Council judged that the work was unfinished and extended the mandate.

The text repeats the mission's tasks and asks for regular reports from the Secretary-General on security and progress. It also stresses that Iraq's government must protect UN staff so they can move around the country. Readers can trace, in these yearly renewals, how the UN's Iraq role shrank as the war wound down.
cia-0000132783: Dated 4 September 1960, Cuba and the Caribbean is a declassified CIA paper that looks at Cuba together with its island neighbors rather than in isolation. Fidel Castro had taken power in Havana the year before, and the title frames Cuba as a regional question. The catalog records no finer subject breakdown, and the v1 summary's claims about Washington's fears go beyond what the title can support. Readers get the paper as released through the CIA Reading Room: a regional assessment from the second autumn of the Cuban revolution.
cia-0000136683: Spanish-language records of Brigade 2506 include this document, dated 2 January 1961. The new year opened with the exile brigade in training, its invasion plan still hidden. The catalog gives the item no subject of its own. Preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, it belongs to the cluster of brigade papers from the first days of January 1961, the operation's final winter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d83: Hull wrote to Stettinius, his acting deputy in Washington, on October 31, 1943, and the letter is Document 83 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Secretary-to-deputy letters of this kind handed the department's work back and forth across the Atlantic during the Moscow trip. The record names the two men and the date. Its contents are stated only in the printed text of the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d183: Hull wrote to Roosevelt again on November 2, 1943, and the letter is Document 183, the last in this run of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two Hull letters in two days closed the Moscow story as the secretary turned for home and the president turned toward Cairo. The record names the parties and the date and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, at the end of the section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d283:
John Paton Davies, political adviser to General Stilwell, wrote a memorandum at Cairo about 22 November 1943 on the political side of the China and Southeast Asia theaters. A copy reached Secretary Hull in Washington at the end of December, and the paper appears to have been prepared for Roosevelt's use.

Davies warns that fighting under the Southeast Asia Command drags America into the colonial problems of the British, Dutch, and French. It invites the charge that American boys die to rebuild other nations' empires. He urges the main Asiatic effort in and from China instead, where the cause is popular and Stilwell's plan gives the Chinese their own land to fight for. North Burma must still be retaken with the British to reopen the land route, but after that, he argues, the ways part.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d383:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a secret telegram from Washington on 27 November 1943 about staffing the European Advisory Commission. The three-power body, agreed at the Moscow Conference, will handle European questions as the war ends, and Britain and Russia have already named their men.

Britain has named Strang and Russia Gusev as their principal representatives. Washington, Hull argues, should not play up the body's importance, but its American member will hold a full-time job and must be fully capable of guarding American interests. He offers three names for Roosevelt's choice: Joseph Grew, Jefferson Caffery, and Herschel Johnson. One doubt is attached: Caffery, ambassador in Rio, may not be spareable from Brazil at this time. Hull asks for the President's instructions.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d483:
A formal report by the Combined Chiefs of Staff, dated December 5, 1943, comes from the heart of the Second Cairo Conference. The chiefs, the senior American and British officers, reported upward to Roosevelt and Churchill as the conference neared its end. The State Department printed the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Reports of this kind gathered the chiefs' joint conclusions into one paper the two leaders could approve. They are among the most important documents a summit produces, because they state what the military advisers of both nations could jointly recommend. For readers, this report shows the combined command speaking with one voice near the close of Cairo.
frus-1944-quebec-d83: Number 83 is one of the editorial notes written by the volume's historians. The Quebec 1944 volume uses them where the wartime file has gaps. Notes summarize missing background or direct readers toward related papers. The setting is the run-up to the second Quebec Conference. In September 1944, Roosevelt and Churchill planned the endgame against Germany and Japan. The note keeps that crowded preparation readable for later readers.
frus-1944-quebec-d183:
The Combined Chiefs met at 10 a.m. on September 14, 1944, approved the previous meeting's conclusions, and settled the directive on control of the strategic bomber forces in Europe. The long item was British participation in the Pacific. Brooke said the British chiefs were disturbed by an American paper on the subject, which predated the plenary session and did not match what the president had accepted there.

The argument narrowed to words and fleets. Words confining the British force's first use to the Southwest Pacific's western flank were deleted by agreement. Cunningham described the balanced force Britain had in mind: some four battleships, five or six large carriers, and about twenty light carriers, self-supporting with its fleet train. King insisted the force must be self-supporting, and asked the British to propose its employment.
frus-1944-quebec-d283:
The memorandum initialed by Roosevelt and Churchill on September 15, 1944, is the Quebec agreement on Germany's future. It opens by calling the disposition of the Ruhr and the Saar an essential feature of preventing renewed German rearmament. Germany's metallurgical, chemical, and electric industries, it notes, convert from peace to war with an ease already impressed on the allies by bitter experience.

Those industries in the Ruhr and Saar would therefore be put out of action and closed down. Injured countries, Russia above all, could remove the machinery they needed to repair their losses. A body under the world organization would supervise the dismantling and prevent any restart by subterfuge. The program, the text concludes, looked forward to converting Germany into a country primarily agricultural and pastoral.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d83:
Progress on Security Council voting was slow, and the President was displeased. Secretary of State Stettinius recorded that mood in a short note to his special assistant, Leo Pasvolsky, on 22 December 1944. The note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Stettinius says he has reported the latest developments to the President in person. The Department is pressing the Russians and the British for an early decision. If both answer yes, he hopes invitations can go out for a March meeting to found the United Nations. The President thought that entirely appropriate, but showed displeasure that things were moving so slowly in this field.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d183:
Lord Halifax sent Stettinius London's true feelings about Count Sforza on 5 December 1944. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, encloses a personal telegram from the Prime Minister dated the day before. It answers American anger over Britain's step in Rome.

There is no question, Churchill writes, of a British veto on Sforza as premier or foreign minister. What is certain is that Sforza will not command the slightest trust or confidence from His Majesty's Government. Halifax adds his own gloss. The State Department's soreness, he has told London, rests chiefly on being given no word before Britain spoke. London's defense is that the matter blew up suddenly, and its man in Rome had to speak at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d283:
The British chiefs accepted the American subject list on 20 January 1945, with one addition about France. Their representatives' memorandum, C. C. S. 765/4, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the United States paper of three days before.

The British Chiefs of Staff agree with the subjects proposed for the next American-British-Soviet staff conference. Their single point concerns the occupation zones item. The French now sit on the European Advisory Commission, and they have already stated their views on taking part in the control of Germany and Austria. Any conclusions the conference reaches on the military side of the zones must therefore take French aspirations into account. Failing that, they must be open to discussion with the French after the conference ends.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d383:
Matthews scribbled the ministers' February 8, 1945 agenda in shorthand: an Austria-Yugoslav boundary for administration, control commissions, reparations the next day, and Iran. On Iran, his notes hold a surprise. There was no dispute, he wrote, over the Soviets getting oil from northern Persia. No obstacle stood against a Russian concession, once Persia was ready to negotiate.

The Western side was ready to say all three powers would press no further until Allied troops withdrew. A statement offered earlier withdrawal, step by step, as the supply route closed. Molotov split the matter in two: oil was one question, troops another and new. The notes catch a bargain half-made.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d483:
French developments lead these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 7, 1945, marked for Hopkins's eyes. Ambassador Caffery reported that Foreign Minister Bidault had shown him the French Dumbarton Oaks committee's first reports. They matched American ideas closely. Our ideas are so similar, Bidault stressed, that it would be wicked to let anything come between us.

Bidault remained troubled, though, by the doings of the captured German general von Paulus under Soviet auspices. He feared they might bear on the Big Three conference. He also made clear his alarm at the idea of a Soviet-dominated government on France's frontier. Grew's digest shows France courting Washington while watching Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d83:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent the State Department a draft protest for Moscow on June 20, 1945. Their memorandum, signed by Admiral Leahy, is document 83 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It asks that the enclosed message go to Ambassador Harriman without delay, for delivery to the Soviet Foreign Office.

The draft says Washington is informed that Soviet authorities are holding back permission for the American advance party to enter Berlin. The needed work on communications and housing should already have begun, it argues, and permission should be granted at once. If it cannot be, the meeting date may have to slip, and the only explanation would be the missing Soviet permission. The blunt threat shows American patience wearing thin over summit logistics.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d183:
Justice Robert Jackson warned against summit debate on war crimes trials in a telegram from London on July 4, 1945. The talks go slowly, Jackson reports, because the Russians have trouble grasping the Anglo-American system of law, and the other side has the same trouble in reverse. He is rather appalled at the thought of the Big Three debating so technical a subject, where small phrases hide important differences. The British suggestion, he is told, aims only to calm Russian suspicion that prosecution is being dodged. If the leaders do take it up, he wants to brief the President and Byrnes in detail first.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d283:

The four governments approved on different days: the United Kingdom on July 12, France on July 16, the Soviet Union on July 21, and the United States on July 24. The note points readers to the official treaty series for the text and its annexed maps. It marks the legal settlement of how Austria would be divided and jointly governed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d383:

It trusted London was not turning against the policy of rooting out spearheads of German economic penetration in the neutral countries of Europe and in Turkey.

The American proposal for joint notes to neutrals, the cable explains, was a holding device until the Control Council could act. Reports from the Iberian Peninsula warned that delay encouraged the assets to slip away. Presenting the notes, Washington added, need not at once raise hard legal questions in the neutral states.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d483:
Poland's new start is outlined in a briefing book extract dated June 29, 1945, summarizing suggested American policy. Policy toward Poland, as defined at Yalta, aims first at a truly democratic government of the Polish people's own choice. It also seeks Poland's rapid return to international life as a United Nation, and her early reconstruction, with mutually beneficial relations restored between the United States and Poland.

The Moscow Polish Commission ended its work on June 22, with agreement among the three Polish groups on a Provisional Government of National Unity. Questions left for immediate consideration, the summary says, include establishing American representation in Poland, and holding free and unfettered elections there.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d583:
One short follow-up cable from Foreign Minister Togo to Ambassador Sato forms document 583 in the Potsdam volume. Dated in the small hours of July 12, 1945, it adds a single point to Togo's main cable of that day. That cable carried the Emperor's wish to send Prince Konoye to Moscow as a peace envoy.

Togo's whole point here is secrecy. When Sato puts the matter to the Soviet side, he must make clear that the subject is to be treated as absolutely secret. Togo says he knows he is presuming in stating this. He mentions it merely to be sure. The two-line cable shows how much weight Tokyo placed on keeping the peace feeler hidden, above all from its own foes in the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d683:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded British word of Soviet demands on Turkey in a memo dated June 18, 1945. It is document 683 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. John Balfour of the British Embassy had called that afternoon.

Balfour left a British report from Istanbul and an aide-memoire on a talk in Moscow. Foreign minister Molotov had told the Turkish ambassador that old questions must be settled before any new Soviet-Turkish treaty. Three items were named. Land ceded by Russia to Turkey in the 1921 treaty was claimed to have been yielded under duress and to need revision. Turkey should cede bases to Russia in the Straits. The Montreux Convention should be revised by agreement between the two states. The Turkish ambassador had answered that his government would not reopen the 1921 treaty, which it held was freely negotiated.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-83:
Charles Bohlen, assistant to the Secretary of State and the delegation's best-known Russian expert, sent this message to President Truman on July 24, 1945. Bohlen served as interpreter and adviser at the Potsdam Conference. His note reached the President while the Big Three talks were in full swing near Berlin.

Short notes from Bohlen carried weight because he heard the Soviet side at first hand. He could flag tone, intent, and shifts in wording across the table. The message forms part of the day-by-day staff record in the second Potsdam volume. It shows how much of the conference ran through a small group of trusted aides.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d783:
Philip Mosely set down this memorandum on July 27, 1945, as document 783. Mosely advised the American representative on the European Advisory Commission in London. The Commission had drafted much of the Germany settlement in advance. His memo joined the second Potsdam volume of the conference papers.

A second Mosely paper in this run shows his steady role. He linked the London planning staff to the Potsdam team. Readers see preparatory work being defended and adapted at the summit. The document shows how long the settlement's roots were: ideas drafted in 1944 faced their test in 1945, carried by the men who wrote them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d883:
Secretary of State James Byrnes and Secretary of War Henry Stimson signed this memorandum for the President on German interim financing. The editors date it between July 25 and July 29, 1945. It follows a July 5 paper that set out agreed views across four agencies.

The two secretaries ask Truman to direct the War Department to buy and first finance essential imports for Germany. They note the department can fund food imports through October loadings. They also stress a limit set by Congress. Funds given for this year may be used only to prevent disease and starvation. A draft letter of instructions for the President is attached.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d983:
Covey Oliver, acting chief of the Division of Economic Security Controls, cabled Emilio Collado on July 17, 1945. He reports the chief development on German external assets: Britain has agreed to join in warnings to neutral governments. In Spain, Franco's state industry body wants to acquire German subsidiary firms, and Madrid has sent its ambassador to raise the matter in Washington.

Oliver adds that France is being pressed to concur in the joint proposal. Washington will likely urge that German assets in Rumania, Hungary, and Bulgaria fall under a four-power trusteeship. It will also object to a Soviet attempt to acquire the German legation buildings in Stockholm. Talks with the Swiss touch on a blocked firm, Scintilla.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1083:
Britain's delegation proposed this closing statement on southeast Europe at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. The three heads of government would voice regret at charges of aggression traded between governments in that region. Fears of violent, one-sided moves to settle questions ahead of the peace treaty are also noted.

The draft declares the three powers strongly opposed to any such attempts. They offend the principles the war was fought for, and the Charter of the United Nations. Governments that suffered together under fascist occupation, the text urges, should settle their differences in peace. Their peoples deserve a time of growth and democratic advance. Bevin apparently withdrew the paper the next day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1183:
Truman wrote to Churchill on 25 July 1945, the day before the British count pushed Churchill out of the summit. The message reached the prime minister on his last full day at Potsdam. By the next evening, Clement Attlee would lead the British team.

The two men's partnership had steered the Western alliance through years of war. This note catches that bond at the moment it changed hands. Miracles and predictions receive natural readings inside Kardec's system. Creation, the fall, and prophecy are retold as stages of spirit growth. hering-guiding-symptoms-vol7-1883:
Seven volumes in by 1883, the Guiding Symptoms had become a fixture of homeopathic libraries. Volume VII holds more of Constantine Hering's lifetime harvest: symptoms proved on the healthy, then checked in the sick room. The entries keep their strict order, region by region through the body.

Reading a remedy here means reading a crowd of small, exact reports. One sign may note the hour a pain strikes, another the side it favors. Hering's marks sort the gold from the sand, lifting the guiding symptoms clear. The series rolls on from his notes, still two years past his death.
dariot-breefe-introduction-1583:
Claude Dariot taught Europe to judge the stars, and Fabian Wither's 1583 English version made his Briefe Introduction the earliest astrology manual in English. Dariot, a French physician, wrote for learners who wanted method, not marvels. Elections, the choosing of lucky times, and nativities, the reading of birth charts, form the core.

Rules, tables, and worked examples guide the student step by step through a judgment. The book seeded the English astrological tradition that William Lilly would inherit a century later. Its plain Tudor English and homely cases show astrology as a working craft of the age, not a courtly game.
im-thurn-among-the-indians-of-guiana-188:
Everard Ferdinand im Thurn traveled in British Guiana as a young magistrate and explorer, living among the Carib and Arawak peoples of the forests and rivers. His 1883 book became the classic early account of the colony's native inhabitants.

Much of the book concerns belief: the peaiman, or shaman, who heals and fights spirits, and the unseen world pressing on daily life. Im Thurn describes hunts, feasts, burials, and myths alongside plants, animals, and journeys into the interior. He wrote with respect for people others dismissed. His observations still anchor the study of Guiana's forest tribes.
bradley-principles-logic-1883:
The Principles of Logic, published in 1883, is F. H. Bradley's great work on logic, written before his fame as a metaphysician. Judgment, inference, and the critique of formal logic are treated from an idealist standpoint, against the textbook tradition of his day.

Bradley argues that judgment is not the joining of two ideas but the referral of an ideal content to reality itself. Formal logic, with its symbols and syllogisms, is weighed and found to float above the thought it claims to govern. The book is dense, witty, and destructive. Logicians still argue with it.
maine-early-law-custom-1883:
Henry Maine published his Dissertations on Early Law and Custom in 1883, gathering his later essays. Maine was by then the elder statesman of historical jurisprudence. The essays state his mature thought on how law grows from custom.

He writes on sovereignty, the king in early law, and the theories of primitive society then in fashion. Maine is skeptical of grand schemes that ignore the records. His comparative eye moves from Rome to India to Ireland. The book closes his career's argument: to know law, study its childhood. Modern legal history still starts its debates where Maine left them.
plos-pone-0003383:

Plants without that enzyme, named ssadh, grew very poorly. Adding a fault in a second enzyme, GABA transaminase or POP2, eased the damage. That rescue shows the two enzymes balance each other in the pathway. The result helps explain how plants keep this bypass under control.
plos-pone-0003483:
Richard M. Cubbon and co-authors weighed diabetes risk after heart events in this 2008 study. Diabetes is linked to worse outcomes after acute coronary syndrome. That added risk may vary with each patient's total risk load. The team split cases into first events and repeat events.

They asked if diabetes raised death rates in both settings alike. Comparing the groups gave a more nuanced risk picture. First and recurrent events do not carry the same meaning. Such detail helps doctors set follow-up care for diabetic heart patients. Heart events remain the top cause of death for people with diabetes.
plos-pone-0003583:

The paper covers the concept, design, and implementation of the array. Large-scale association studies were its intended use. A shared platform lets many teams hunt cardiac risk genes comparably. Purpose-built tools can beat generic genome scans for one disease area. Heart gene hunts need very large samples, which shared chips make cheaper.
plos-pone-0003683:

Their responses lean away from the Th1 style that fights microbes inside cells. That gap has slowed work on infant vaccines.

The team tested a vaccine with the antigens Ag85B and ESAT-6 in the adjuvant IC31. Given to newborns, it drew T cell and dendritic cell responses much like those of adults. Such adult-like responses at birth are a step toward tuberculosis vaccines that protect from the start of life.
plos-pone-0003783:

Faults in a protein called eIF2B cause a childhood disease where brain white matter vanishes under stress. The protein helps start the making of new proteins in cells. Oligodendrocytes are the cells that build myelin.

The team studied a point mutation in eIF2B in cells derived from oligodendroglia. The single change left the cells in a continuous hyper stress state. That constant alarm helps explain why myelin is lost when the body is stressed in this disease.
plos-pone-0003883:

Many such patients also have blocked leg arteries, called peripheral arterial disease. That leg problem often gets in the way of rehab exercise programs.

The authors compared new rehab plans that also find and treat the leg disease. They asked whether the added care pays for itself in health gained. Cost studies of this kind help clinics choose programs they can afford. The work speaks to hospitals planning rehab for patients with both heart and vessel disease.
plos-pone-0003983:

Some brain theories still predict millisecond-accurate patterns can emerge. Networks might use such precision as a code.

Their PLOS ONE article weighs the statistical significance of repeated patterns. Recordings came from synapses inside cells in their experiments. Precise repeats beyond chance would support timing-based coding. The study gives other labs a method to judge pattern claims. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004083:

Their vomeronasal-type receptors sit in the main smell tissue instead. Odorant and trace amine receptors share that same tissue.

Their PLOS ONE article traces evolutionary patterns across receptor gene families. It also weighs the selective pressures shaping each family. Fish smell systems reorganized as vertebrates moved between water and land. Comparing families clarifies what pheromone sensing does in fish. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004183:
Weiping Qin and colleagues published this Alzheimer's study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia in older people. There is no cure, and there were no early diagnostic tests when this study appeared. So the hunt for a biomarker, a measurable sign of disease, was urgent.

The team studied S100A7, a protein they put forward as a novel biomarker. They report that it acts by selectively boosting ADAM-10, an enzyme that cuts the amyloid precursor protein in the safer, non-amyloid route. One protein thus offers both a possible early sign of disease and a clue to slowing it.
plos-pone-0004283:
Robert De Lisle and colleagues published this cystic fibrosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cystic fibrosis affects the gastrointestinal tract in many ways, and poor nutrition is a common problem. In the CF mouse, an innate immune response floods the small intestine's muscle wall with mast cells. The same mice show disordered movement of the gut.

The team examined how those mast cells relate to the gastrointestinal dysmotility, the faulty movement of food through the gut. Separating cause from bystander matters, because mast cells can be targeted by existing drugs.
plos-pone-0004383:
Malaria still kills many children across Africa each year. Tools that cut contact with mosquitoes save lives now. Azra Ghani, Colin Sutherland, Eleanor Riley, and co-authors asked a longer question in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper weighs what happens to group immunity when exposure falls. It also asks how that change can distort readings of disease trends.

People in high-malaria areas build partial immunity through repeated infection. Cut exposure, and that shield can fade over time. Later case counts may then shift for reasons beyond control efforts alone. The authors argue trends must be read with immunity loss in mind. Their warning supports steady, lasting control rather than short campaigns.

plos-pone-0004683: In 2009, a team found home life shaping young autistic kids' speech anew here. Home factors shaped speech growth in young autistic kids. The home world mattered quite greatly here. The study informs speech therapy design today. The nature-nurture mix is key here.

crabbe-village-1783:
Crabbe's Village, issued in 1783 with The Newspaper beside it, was the poem that made his name. He wrote it as a direct reply to pretty, false pictures of country life in the verse of his day. Dr. Johnson himself helped polish the draft before it reached print, by the v1 account.

In place of singing shepherds, Crabbe shows poverty, grinding labor, sickness, and early death among the poor. The companion piece turns the same blunt eye on the press and its habits. Side by side, the two poems announced a new kind of poet, one who insisted on telling the truth.
zola-ladies-paradise-1883:
Hutchinson issued The Ladies' Paradise at London in 1895, in Vizetelly's free English rendering. His opening essay warns readers not to fear the book's sound moral. He traces a drift toward joint ventures and near monopolies in modern trade.

A giant Paris shop, glittering and ruthless, swallows small traders street by street. Young Denise comes from the provinces to work inside that bright machine. She survives its harsh rivalries through goodness and grit. Owner Mouret, a genius of selling, remakes shopping itself around her. Love story and business epic in one, the novel stands as the first great tale of consumer capitalism.
green-conquest-of-england-1883:
John Richard Green tells of England's conquest and remaking in The Conquest of England, from 1883. Danish kings rule first, then Cnut and the Godwin family hold the land. The tale ends in 1071, amid the Norman aftermath of Hastings.

Green wrote history from the people's side, not the palace's alone. Towns, laws, and daily life matter as much as battles in his pages. He traced how a nation absorbs its conquerors and stays itself. The book stands as a classic of history from below for the medieval age, learned yet warm, and full of sympathy for ordinary English folk.
braid-neurypnologie-1883:
James Braid's Neurypnology reaches French readers in this 1883 translation of his founding work on hypnotism. The Manchester surgeon strips mesmerism of magnets and mystery fluids. Trance, he shows, is a nervous sleep brought on by fixed gaze and tired attention, a state of the subject's own brain.

Braid coined the very word hypnotism for the new science he claimed. His calm method won doctors where stage wonders had won only crowds. The French dress carried his ideas across the Channel to new schools. The book marks the birth of hypnotism as a science, a turning point in the study of mind.
las-casas-spanish-colonie-1583:
English readers first met Las Casas in The Spanish Colonie, printed in 1583. An unnamed translator Englished the Brevísima relación for an Elizabethan audience. The short book brought Spain's crimes in the Indies home to London readers.

Its grim tales of cruelty fed what later ages call the Black Legend. English readers used the tract as proof of Spanish cruelty abroad. At the same time, its moral charge went far past mere propaganda. The pamphlet warned England what empire could do to its soul. Few short books have shaped two nations' views of each other so long.
treaty-of-paris-1783:
Signed in Paris in 1783, the treaty ended the American Revolutionary War between the United States and Great Britain. Britain formally accepted that the thirteen colonies were now an independent nation. The new country's borders ran from the Atlantic coast to the Mississippi River, and from Canada down to Florida.

Inside, the terms cover fishing rights, debts owed on both sides, and the fair treatment of Americans who had stayed loyal to Britain. The text also promised that Britain would withdraw its troops without delay. It stands as the founding diplomatic act of the American republic, the moment independence became real on paper after eight years of war.

The five volumes before it had printed the whole of Bracton's thirteenth-century treatise on English law, in Latin with an English translation. A work of that size needed tools to make it usable, and the final volume supplies them.

Here are the full index, the glossaries of hard legal terms, and the rest of the editor's working apparatus. A reader can trace any rule, case, or Latin phrase across the entire treatise in minutes. The volume is the key to the whole set, the map that turns six heavy books into one searchable system. It completes the Victorian edition that legal scholars relied on for the next generation.
jevons-methods-social-reform-1883:
Methods of Social Reform and Other Papers came out in 1883, the year after Jevons's death. It collects the essays in which the great theorist of marginal utility turned to practical questions. Jevons had strong views on how the state should, and should not, try to improve working-class life.

The papers treat labor unions, education, public libraries, and the proper limits of state action. Jevons favors experiment and local trial over grand schemes, testing each proposal against evidence. His famous caution about the dangers of state socialism runs beside a real sympathy for workers' aims. The volume shows economics with its sleeves rolled up: the abstract thinker of value theory judging concrete evils and concrete cures. It remains a sharp statement of Victorian liberal reform at its most thoughtful.

Menger, the Viennese founder of the Austrian school, had already recast value theory in his Principles of 1871. The new book defends the method behind that theory against the German historical school, opening the famous battle of methods, the Methodenstreit.

Menger argues that economics can state exact laws, much as the natural sciences do, and that history alone cannot supply them. He sorts the social sciences into kinds and gives each its proper task. The historical school answered hotly, and the quarrel split German-speaking economics for a generation. Menger's side of the argument, stated with the founder's authority, shaped the Austrian tradition down to Mises and Hayek. The book remains its methodological charter.

Its home field is artificial intelligence (the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data). The paper presents new research for specialists to read, test, and build upon.
plos-pone-0005383: Lasting illnesses like tuberculosis resist treatment, partly because germs hide. Eswarappa used game theory to analyze where pathogens locate during lasting illnesses. The strategic lens shows hiding patterns. Math hunting germs in their hideouts, a new application of game theory to infectious sickness.
plos-pone-0005483: South Africa's program to stop babies getting HIV generates mountains of data. Mate and colleagues examined data-management challenges in the PMTCT program. The operational research guides health-system strengthening. Data plumbing for saving newborns at national scale, implementation science for a critical public-health goal.
plos-pone-0005583: Ovarian cancer ascites is rich in LPA, which may drive the disease. Murph and colleagues showed LPA-induced gene profiles match serous ovarian carcinoma and predict worse prognosis. The lipid signal marks aggressive tumors. A fatty signal of poor outcomes identified.
plos-pone-0005683: HIV escapes CCR5-blocking drugs through viral evolution. Tsibris and colleagues used deep sequencing to track HIV escape during antagonist therapy. The quasispecies shifts are dramatic. Watching the virus wriggle free, read by read, deep sequencing for drug-resistance surveillance, across four patients and millions of viral reads.
plos-pone-0005783: Madagascar's forests face poverty-driven tree loss. Brooks and team studied census and markets driving tree loss near Ranomafana. The analysis links group growth to forest loss. Safety money on the ground, in Madagascar, poverty and living variety clashing, highland forests' unique flora, policy-apt tree loss science.
plos-pone-0006383: Eye jumps warp what we see. Noritake and team found fast eye moves squeeze seen shapes toward the jump target. Boxes resist the squeeze; Kanizsa figures do not. Now you see it, now you do not — vision's jumpy gaps, where dots alone dodge the squeeze.
plos-pone-0006483: Doctors need a quick risk read. Penel and team built a bedside score for early death risk in mystery-origin cancers. The score guides hard calls — a number for tough news, checked, in 429 patients. Ninety-day window, single center: math picked signs.
plos-pone-0006583: DNA traced bombers' roots. Phillips and team used origin DNA to aid the Madrid train bombing probe. The genes pointed north — crime lab's origin compass, mapped, for the 11-M attacks. 2004 bombings, second biggest in Europe: STR profiles, complex case, Spain's biggest.
plos-pone-0009383: Inside every cell, proteins must fold into precise shapes; misfolded ones clump into toxic aggregates that damage the cell. This research paper maps which proteins in a bacterium's inner fluid are most likely to clump and why. The authors find that the tendency to aggregate is written into each protein's own building blocks, a result that could sharpen how scientists study diseases caused by misfolding.
plos-pone-0009483: Esophageal adenocarcinoma has surged in the US, and scientists needed a virtual laboratory to study why. This paper builds, calibrates, and validates a mathematical simulation of the disease in US white men, the hardest-hit group. The model lets researchers test what drives the rise — and what interventions could bend the curve — without waiting decades.
plos-pone-0009583: Most of the 10 million annual child deaths happen where no doctor records a cause. This study of 27,000 verbal autopsies in India tests how well physicians agree on causes of death from family interviews. The paper validates a crucial tool for counting — and ultimately preventing — invisible child deaths.
plos-pone-0010383: Fruit fly wings get their veins from a tug-of-war between two signaling pathways. This study shows Smad2 pushes back against Mad signaling as wing veins form. The paper reveals how balanced opposition sculpts a precise pattern, a lesson in developmental checks and balances.
plos-pone-0010483: Telling which of two sensations came first is a basic brain job. This study tracks c-Fos activity in mice performing a timing task. The paper maps the brain regions that order our senses in time. The maps show timing is a whole-brain computation.
plos-pone-0010583: People carry memory T cells that recognize many flu strains at once. But the flu's nucleoprotein keeps mutating — and this study asks how much those changes erode cross-strain protection. The answer sets limits. The paper measures how far our cellular immunity can stretch.
plos-pone-0010683: In temporal lobe epilepsy, the brain's wiring tips toward seizures. This mouse study shows cannabis-like compounds quiet overactive excitatory loops in the dentate gyrus. The paper maps where the calming happens. The finding explains how these compounds settle electrical storms.
plos-pone-0010783: Little brown bats are dying by the millions from a cold-loving fungus. This study characterizes Geomyces destructans, the psychrophilic culprit behind white-nose syndrome in New York bats. The paper identifies the killer. The work guides the fight to save North America's bats.
plos-pone-0010883: Catching insulin resistance early could prevent diabetes. This study finds alpha-hydroxybutyrate rises early in nondiabetic people heading toward trouble. The paper offers a warning biomarker. The test could trigger timely lifestyle change. The early signal beats current tests to the punch.
plos-pone-0010983: Danger signals push dendritic cells to mature. This study tests how TLR agonists affect the hypoxia factor HIF-1alpha during maturation under normal oxygen. The paper reveals unexpected crosstalk. The finding informs vaccine adjuvant design. The unexpected crosstalk rewrites dendritic-cell textbooks.
plos-pone-0011083: Tiny preemies need gut watchdogs. This study measures a stool marker called calprotectin in premature babies during their first weeks. The paper sets a baseline for gut health. The finding could flag dangerous gut disease early. The early flag could save fragile newborn lives.
plos-pone-0011183: Counting the dead accurately matters where records don't exist. This study tests a verbal autopsy questionnaire's reliability for causes of death in Iran's Golestan cohort. The paper validates the method. The finding strengthens mortality statistics. The statistics guide health policy.
plos-pone-0011283: Practicing timing with two senses sharpens vision alone. This study shows multisensory perceptual learning of temporal order transfers to vision but not audition. The paper reveals a sensory asymmetry. The finding informs brain training. The brain training targets the right sense.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1283:
On 17 July 1945, the day the conference opened, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Notes of this kind put the staff's analysis on paper so leaders could decide. The chiefs' office began its Potsdam file as the talks began.

An opening-day memorandum holds the services' first framing of the questions. Later papers in the run react to deals and drafts; this one stands before them. Its value lies in that clean starting point. It shows what the American military staff thought the summit had to settle, before the bargaining taught anyone otherwise.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1383:
The Protocol of the Proceedings of the Berlin Conference, dated 1 August 1945, is the Potsdam summit's own signed record of its choices. Truman, Attlee, and Stalin set their names to the results it lists. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Inside, readers find the core bargain of 1945: how Germany would be run, where Poland's borders would lie, and how reparations would be drawn. The protocol is dry, dense, and of the first rank among the century's papers. Every cable and proposal earlier in the volume leads toward it or flows from it. Anyone who reads one Potsdam text in full should start with this statement of what the three powers agreed.
frus-1945-50-intel-d83:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 31 December 1945, closing the year for the State intelligence office. He had run the office since it rose from the OSS research branch in September. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A New Year's Eve memorandum from an office chief to his secretary reads like a report and a plea in one. McCormack knew the central settlement coming in January would fix his office's place, and not at the center. Readers can set his December paper beside his hopeful October letters from Byrnes. The arc between them, favor to foreboding in one season, is the State intelligence office's whole story in brief.
frus-1945-50-intel-d183:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 18" heads a text dated 23 January 1947. It is document 183 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

A numbered directive joined a growing shelf of rules that told the new agencies how to run themselves. Staff could be held to each line, which is why the words were fought over before issue. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d283:
On 3 June 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 12th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 283 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Staff trusted these notes because they were made at once, and files across Washington cite them as the record of a talk. For a reader, the gain is scene and voice, rare goods in a file of stiff forms. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d383:
A memorandum dated 27 April 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was Secretary of Defense Johnson. The reader was the Secretaries of the Army (Royall), the Navy (Sullivan) and the Air Force (Symington). It stands as document 383 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The debate now was about reform: the Dulles survey had judged the CIA, and the replies and counter-replies were piling up.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1861-d83:
On 14 September 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London.

The crossing letters of 14 September are a neat emblem of the whole run. Chief and envoy each pushed his view of the week across the sea. Their two files, read side by side, show a partnership built on trust and ink. Few chief and envoy pairs in the record match their trust and pace. Their pace that autumn never slackened, though the news gave them little cheer. Their paired pages remain a neat emblem of trust built by mail.
frus-1861-d183:
Carl Schurz sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 October 1861. It is document 183 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz's third October letter in the file keeps the pace of a post in full swing. Madrid's stance held steady, and he could report it plainly. Such steady word from Spain freed Seward to spend his care on London and Paris. Steady word from Spain let the cabinet spend its fear where fear was due. Fear spent where it was due was the cabinet's goal through that hard autumn.
frus-1861-d283:
From abroad on 28 July 1861, Mr. Haldeman sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 283 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d83:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 23 June 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 83 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d183:
The second of three Seward letters dated 4 November 1862 stands as Document 183 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Its destination was the London legation, where Charles Francis Adams served as American minister to Britain.

Historians value these dense clusters of mail because they expose how orders were built, topic by topic, before a steamer sailed. A single short dispatch may look slight on its own. Set among its mates, it helps show the full brief Adams carried into his talks with Earl Russell that month. Cotton hunger in British mill towns kept the war a kitchen-table topic across the North of England.
frus-1862-d283:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch on 3 June 1862, printed as Document 283 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It answered into the steady stream of Paris reports.

Seward wrote as the siege of Richmond settled in and the North waited for a decision in Virginia. His guidance to Dayton balanced patience with warning: France should not mistake a long war for a lost one. Letters of this kind, calm in tone and firm in substance, were the Secretary's chief tool in Europe that summer. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d383:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to Simon Cameron on 23 July 1862. In a dispatch printed as Document 383 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron had succeeded Cassius Clay as American minister in Russia.

The same date carries a Cameron report, so the two papers likely crossed in transit. Cameron, a former secretary of war, took the St. Petersburg post in mid-1862. Seward's July dispatch belongs to the channel's change of hands, when Washington refreshed its instructions for a court whose friendship it prized. The legation's quiet year was the exception in a volume full of friction.
frus-1862-d483:
James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands, opened the Dutch file with this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 January 1862. It is Document 483 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Pike was a Maine journalist and antislavery man whom Lincoln sent to The Hague. The Netherlands was a trading nation with colonies in the East and West Indies, and its ports and insurers felt the war's effects at once. His January report told Washington how the Dutch government and press read the conflict after the Trent affair. The letter begins one of the volume's fullest small-country files.
frus-1862-d583:
On 20 March 1862 Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 583 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

By March the allied expedition in Mexico was splitting apart, as France's larger aims showed through the debt-collecting cover. Corwin, living in the capital of the threatened republic, sent Washington the view from the ground. His sympathy for Juárez's government was open, and his reports argued the American interest in keeping Mexico independent. For readers, the Corwin file is the volume's most dramatic American correspondence, written from a neighboring capital while European armies operated on its soil.
frus-1862-d683:
On 26 November 1861, William Sydney Thayer sent this report from Egypt to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Thayer served as the American consul general there. The dispatch is document 683 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Egypt's cotton had shot up in worth once the war cut off the South's crop, and ports like Alexandria felt the change fast. A consul's letters tracked prices, ships, and the acts of the viceroy's government. Thayer's dispatch is part of that watch. It shows how a trade post at the edge of the war still fed facts that mattered in Washington.
frus-1863p1-d83:
On 14 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. A second letter to Adams in the volume bears the same date. An older one of the same day and month sits just before them. This letter is document 83 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Seward's mid-February mail kept the London brief in motion. The standing work was to hold Britain to fair dealing and to choke off the warships rising in its yards for the South. This letter is one of the day's pair on that work. It shows the secretary's steady hand, writing the same claims in fresh forms as the news changed.
frus-1863p1-d183:
From Washington on 5 May 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 183 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d283:
Washington's orders to London on 5 September 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 283 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d383:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 February 1863. His note is document 383 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Under the formal courtesy sits real tension: a neutral Britain trading with both sides, and a Union government sure that trade kept the South alive. This exchange is where the two views met. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d483:
Document 483, dated 28 April 1863, records a letter from the State Department's chief clerk, W. Hunter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d583:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington received a letter dated 2 July 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d683:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to London on 15 December 1863, near the end of the year. His letter to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in Britain, is document 683 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume.

Year-end letters often took stock, and Washington had much to weigh. The Union held more ground, but the war was far from over, and Britain's stance still counted. Seward kept the flow of news and orders steady so Adams would not have to guess. For the reader, this note marks where the long exchange stood as 1863 closed. It gains force when read with the notes around it.
plos-pbio-0000083:
Keiichi Kondo, William Y. Kim, Mirna Lechpammer, and their team reported a cancer finding in PLOS Biology in 2003. Some kidney tumors grow after the VHL gene is lost. That loss lets a protein called HIF2α build up and push tumor growth forward.

The authors asked a sharp question: is HIF2α the main driver, or just one of many? Their tests show that blocking HIF2α alone is enough to stop these tumors from growing. That narrows a complex pathway to one key target. For drug research, the message is direct. A treatment that lowers HIF2α action might help patients whose tumors lack working VHL.
plos-pbio-0020383:
Stuart H. M. Butchart, Alison J. Stattersfield, and a huge team built a trend index for birds in PLOS Biology in 2004. The Red List ranks species by extinction risk. The team tracked how bird species move between ranks over time. From that, they made an index of whether bird life is gaining or losing.

The index fell, showing birds slipping toward extinction faster than they recovered. A single number that sums thousands of species accounts is a strong tool for policy. Governments had pledged to slow biodiversity loss, and this index lets the world check their progress. Birds were the test case, with like indices for other groups soon to follow.
plos-pone-0000083:
Domenico Girelli, Nicola Martinelli, Oliviero Olivieri, and a large team studied heart surgery outcomes in PLOS ONE in 2006. High blood levels of homocysteine, an amino acid by-product, mark a state called hyperhomocysteinemia. The team checked whether patients with high levels fared worse after coronary artery bypass grafting.

In their group, high homocysteine went with higher death rates after surgery. A blood marker that flags risk before an operation is useful: it can guide watchfulness and care after the graft. The result also adds to the long debate on homocysteine and heart disease. Whether lowering it with vitamins helps remains a separate question the data invite.
plos-pone-0000183:
Philip C. Hill, David J. Jeffries, Roger H. Brookes, and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Contacts of TB patients are checked with skin tests, but a positive result can be a false alarm. The authors use ELISPOT, a blood test that spots immune cells reacting to TB, to expose such false positive conversions.

A skin test that flips positive wrongly can trigger months of needless preventive treatment. Comparing the two tests in the same contacts shows where the skin test misleads. The work supports using blood-based tests to confirm conversions, sharpening TB control programs that track transmission through households.
plos-pone-0000283:
Mathieu Paoletti, Sven J. Saupe, and Corinne Clavé published this fungal genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fungi can tell self from non-self, rejecting tissue from genetically different individuals of the same species. The authors study the genesis, the evolutionary origin, of the repertoire of genes behind that non-self recognition.

A recognition repertoire must be diverse enough to tell many strains apart. Tracing how that diversity arose shows how fungi built an immune-like system without antibodies. The work bears on fungal biology and on the general question of how self-recognition systems evolve.
plos-pone-0000383:
Feng Chen and colleagues compared computer methods for spotting orthologs, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Orthologs are genes in different species that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. Finding them correctly is a basic step in comparing genomes and tracing how genes evolved.

Several detection strategies exist, and they do not always agree. The team assessed how well the strategies perform when applied to eukaryotic genomes, the DNA of organisms with cell nuclei, from yeast to humans. Benchmarks like this help researchers choose tools they can trust, and they show where methods still mistake look-alike genes for true counterparts.
plos-pone-0000483:
Cesare Massone and colleagues proposed an everyday device as a skin cancer screening tool, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was melanoma screening with cellular phones: using phone cameras and messaging to capture images of suspicious moles and send them for expert review.

Melanoma is curable when caught early and dangerous when late, yet dermatologists are scarce in many regions. A phone-based screen could extend expert eyes to distant patients cheaply. In 2007, phone cameras were still crude, so the idea was forward-looking. The study tested whether the images were good enough to base triage decisions on.
plos-pone-0000583:
Dinesh Adhikary and colleagues prepared immune cells aimed at a lifelong virus, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Epstein-Barr virus infects most people and hides in their cells for life. The team studied Epstein-Barr virus-specific CD4+ T cell preparations made for therapy. They asked which lytic cycle antigens dominate. In other words, which viral proteins do the therapeutic T cells mainly recognize?

Cell therapy grows a patient's own T cells against the virus and returns them, a strategy used when drugs fail. Knowing which antigens dominate the response tells makers whether their product aims at the right targets. Lytic antigens come from the virus's active phase, relevant when it reactivates in immune-suppressed patients.
plos-pone-0000683:
Marcella Funicello, Michela Novelli, Maurizio Ragni and co-authors studied mice lacking a fat-related enzyme for PLOS ONE in 2007. Proteases, proteins that cut other proteins, are implicated in fat formation and the onset of obesity. The team had reported that one cysteine protease, cathepsin K, is overexpressed in the white fat tissue of obese individuals.

Here they characterized the fat tissue of mice with the cathepsin K gene knocked out. The title states the result: during the rapid buildup of fat stores, these mice showed reduced adiposity. Linking one protease to fat gain suggests a drug target, and it reshapes how fat tissue growth is understood.
plos-pone-0000783:
Alberto Viera, Rocío Gómez, María T. Parra and colleagues watched a chromosome-shaping complex at work in mouse meiosis, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Chromosomes must be shaped and individualized so genomes segregate correctly in mitotic and meiotic divisions. In vertebrates, three multiprotein complexes drive that shaping: cohesin and condensins I and II. Meiosis, the division making sperm and eggs, has its own special chromosome choreography.

Their title promises new insights from condensin I on mouse meiotic chromosome structure and dynamics. Errors in meiosis cause infertility and conditions such as Down syndrome. Knowing which complex does what, and when, fills a basic gap in reproductive biology.
plos-pone-0000883:
Michael Lombardo, Jennifer Barnes, Sally Wheelwright and co-authors tested self-focused thought and empathy in autism, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. People on the autism spectrum often find social life hard. Whether they also differ when thinking about themselves, rather than about others, was much less clear.

The team used several well tested measures to compare self-referential cognition, thinking tied to oneself, with empathy for others. Keeping those two domains apart matters: a person can struggle with one and not the other. The study helps refine what autism affects, and what it may leave intact. That sharper picture can guide fairer tests and better support.
plos-pone-0000983:
Aparna Nittala, Soumitra Ghosh and Xujing Wang modeled how the layout of insulin cells shapes their rhythm, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Insulin leaves the pancreas in pulses, and that pulsing is basic to healthy blood sugar control. The pulses come from beta cells in each islet firing together, coupled to their neighbors.

The team built a new beta cell cluster model to ask what islet cytoarchitecture, the physical arrangement of the cells, does to the oscillation. Arrangement is easy to overlook beside chemistry. Yet if layout tunes the rhythm, then damage to islet structure in diabetes matters in its own right, not just cell loss.
plos-pone-0001083:
Dan Valente, Ilan Golani and Partha Mitra analyzed how fruit flies move in a circular arena, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Describing the full behavior of a freely moving animal is hard. Yet studies of the brain and behavior need exactly such records.

Existing metrics for movement are partial at best. They capture speed or turning, but not the whole pattern. The team present an analysis of the fly's trajectory as a complete record. Drosophila is the workhorse of genetics, so a rigorous behavior language for it serves many labs. Their approach treats the path itself as the phenotype to be explained.
plos-pone-0001183:
Diabetes often comes with reduced thyroid function and poor muscle repair after injury. Bernhard Baumgartner and colleagues went looking for a missing piece of thyroid hormone action in muscle, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They identified a gene, named DOR, that is abundant in insulin-sensitive tissues and is repressed in diabetic rat muscle.

The authors describe DOR as a novel modulator of thyroid hormone receptor-mediated action. A modulator is a protein that tunes how strongly a hormone's receptor works. Finding one that diabetes turns down connects two features of the disease, low thyroid action and weak muscle regeneration, in a single mechanism.
plos-pone-0001283:
Chuuk State, in the Federated States of Micronesia, saw its first two locally acquired HIV infections, and health officials moved to assess the risk. Toya Russell and colleagues surveyed sexual risk behaviors there, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The purpose was to assess the need for HIV education and prevention services and to develop recommendations for those services.

Remote, at-risk populations are often reached only after an epidemic is established. This study gathered first evidence before that happened in Chuuk. Its case is for early prevention fitted to a small island population.
plos-pone-0001383:
Vladimir Hampl and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a tiny single celled creature called Trimastix. Most complex cells hold small power plants called mitochondria. A few gut parasites were once thought to lack them and to have split off before such plants arose. Trimastix was one of those cases.

The team found gene proof that Trimastix did once have such power plants. Its stock of genes fits a past with them, not a past without them. That shifts where this creature sits on the tree of life. It also adds weight to the view that all complex cells share one root that held these power plants.
plos-pone-0001483:
Héctor Pálmer and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on skin growth signals. Two signals, one from the Wnt path and one from vitamin D, jointly steer how skin cells mature. Many skin genes switched on by the Wnt path carry vitamin D response marks. The team traced how the two signals share control of hair growth.

They show the vitamin D receptor acts as a Wnt effector in skin. It helps set how hair base cells mature and which tumor type forms in adult skin. That dual role was not in the standard account. It may guide new care for hair loss and skin tumors alike.
plos-pone-0001583:
Lisa Lindqvist and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the first drug aimed at one RNA helicase. Helicases unwind RNA and serve in making proteins, splicing, and RNA decay. They have little aim by nature, so blocking just one was a hard task. The team sought a drug that hits a single helicase tied to protein making.

They report a compound that does pick out that one helicase. A first in class drug proves the family can be drugged with aim. Such drugs could serve as probes, and in time as cures for ills where this helicase runs high. The work opens a new shelf in drug design.
plos-pone-0001683:
Michael J. Stringer, Marta Sales-Pardo, and Luís A. Nunes Amaral tested how well journal rankings help scientists find information, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Electronic publishing, preprint archives, blogs, and wikis had raised doubts about the place of journals and peer review. If readers can find anything online, do ranked journal lists still guide them to what matters?

The authors measured the effectiveness of ranking schemes as search tools. The full text gives their model of how scientists search, the rankings tested, and how often each scheme led readers to relevant work. The results feed a live debate about how science sorts its own flood of papers, and whether prestige rankings serve readers or mainly reward journals.
plos-pone-0001783:

Leonardo Vairo, an Italian churchman, published De fascino, on fascination, in Latin in 1583. Three books study the evil eye, the belief that a mere look can sicken children, spoil milk, or wither love. Vairo treats its species and causes with scholastic care and many examples.

Anton van Dale, a Dutch physician and scholar, published his two dissertations on the heathen oracles in Latin in 1683. He asks how long the oracles of Greece and Rome truly lasted, and who really spoke through them. His answers demolished the reigning theory that demons had talked from the shrines.

Van Dale shows priestcraft at work. The oracles, he argues, were human frauds kept up for gain, and they ended with politics, not with Christ's birth. Fontenelle later popularized the argument in French, and the Enlightenment ran with it. Van Dale's Latin remains the source. Few scholarly books have so quietly rearranged what educated Europe believed.
